passage: “Himani, how big was the balloon at the party?” asked Sarita. Himani spread her arms as wide as they would go and puffed her cheeks. “Big!” “So big!” said Sarita. At dinner Himani cupped both hands together and held them up. “You want a bowl?” Sarita passed her steel bowl, and Himani beamed and held it out toward the pot of dal. Then she pointed at the high shelf, palm open, stretching. “The biscuit tin? You did well showing me.”

qa.q: How did Himani show the size of the balloon?
qa.a: She spread her arms as wide as they would go.

qa.q: What do Himani's stretched arms and cupped hands seem to say about how she feels?
qa.a: They show pride in describing the balloon and a wish for the bowl and the biscuits. She might also be enjoying showing Sarita that she can make herself understood.

qa.q: How could Sarita help Himani's language grow?
qa.a: Sarita could say aloud what the gestures mean, like “big balloon” and “bowl, please”, and then wait for Himani to try the words.

qa.q: How might Himani feel when Sarita understands her gestures?
qa.a: She may feel proud and understood, and want to communicate even more. 😊

grounding: A toddler stretches her arms wide for big, cups her hands for a bowl and reaches for a wanted object, and an adult names the meaning.

passage:
“Nitin, what did you see at the zoo?” asked Varun.
Nitin stretched both arms wide. “Big!”
“A big elephant?”
Nitin nodded, then held cupped hands to his mouth.
“And it drank water?”
“Wa-wa,” said Nitin, looking pleased.
He reached out to the toy shelf, fingers opening and closing.
“The toy elephant? Here.” Varun handed it over. Nitin held it up high in both hands, chin up.

qa.q: What did Nitin show with both arms stretched wide?
qa.a: That the elephant at the zoo was big.

qa.q: What do Nitin's raised chin and held-up elephant suggest he feels?
qa.a: They suggest pride that he could tell Varun about the zoo. He might also just be pleased to have the toy.

qa.q: What could Varun say to help Nitin's speech?
qa.a: Varun could repeat the gestures in words, such as “big elephant” and “drinks water”, and let Nitin copy them.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel when Varun guesses the elephant?
qa.a: He may feel understood and excited, because his messages without words worked.

grounding: A toddler stretches his arms wide for big, cups his hands and reaches for a wanted toy, and an adult names the meaning.

passage: Playgroup note, Monday. Jeevan came in bursting to tell me something with no words yet. He stretched his arms out as wide as they would go and made a rumbling noise. "A big, big truck?" I said. He nodded hard, chest out. Later at snack time he cupped both hands together and held them out. "A bowl? You want your bowl?" Another nod. Naming it aloud seemed to please him. Harsha, playgroup teacher

qa.q: What noise did Jeevan make with his arms stretched wide?
qa.a: A rumbling noise.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when he nodded hard with his chest out?
qa.a: He seemed proud and excited that Harsha understood his big-truck story.

qa.q: What habit of Harsha's could help Jeevan's words grow?
qa.a: Naming each gesture aloud, such as "a big, big truck" or "your bowl", so Jeevan hears the words for what he shows.

qa.q: How might Jeevan's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would likely feel happy and proud to learn how Jeevan is telling stories with his hands.

grounding: A teacher names a toddler's wide-arm and cupped-hand gestures aloud, meeting his pride and wants with words.

passage:
Arnab came up from the village pond with two fish on a string. Raghav toddled ahead of him into the house, straight to Maa, and stretched his arms wide, wide, wide.
"A big fish?" Maa asked.
Raghav nodded, then pinched his fingers close together and pointed at Arnab.
"And a small one too!" Arnab laughed, holding up the tiny one. Raghav bounced, arms wide again, looking from Maa to his brother.

qa.q: How many fish did Arnab bring up from the pond?
qa.a: Two fish on a string.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling as he stretched his arms wide for Maa?
qa.a: He was excited and proud to share the news of the big fish, bouncing and looking from Maa to his brother.

qa.q: How did Maa and Arnab help Raghav's language here?
qa.a: They put words to his gestures, "a big fish" and "a small one too", matching his wide arms and pinched fingers.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel seeing Raghav tell the story?
qa.a: Arnab likely feels amused and proud that his little brother is so excited about his catch.

grounding: A toddler uses wide arms and pinched fingers to show big and little, and his family names the meaning aloud.

passage:
At the drinking fountain in a Montreal park, Nour strained up on her toes, one arm reaching, fingers opening and closing. Jin, her neighbour, was walking her home.
"You want water?" Jin asked. Nour nodded and cupped both hands together under the spout.
Jin pressed the button. Water filled her tiny cupped hands and spilled everywhere. Nour squealed and cupped them again, looking up proudly.

qa.q: Where were Nour and Jin?
qa.a: At the drinking fountain in a Montreal park.

qa.q: What did Nour's proud look up at Jin show?
qa.a: She felt proud and delighted at catching water in her own cupped hands, and wanted Jin to see.

qa.q: What did Jin do that helped Nour?
qa.a: Jin named what her reaching meant, "You want water?", and helped her get it.

qa.q: How might it feel for Jin when Nour squeals?
qa.a: It likely feels fun and warm to see her so pleased with her small success. 😊

grounding: A toddler reaches for a fountain and cups her hands, and an adult names her want aloud.

passage:
I'm Rajni, Gautam's cousin. I was at their house for the temple festival.
When the elephant walked past the gate, Gautam stretched his arms as wide as they'd go and looked at his mother.
“Yes! Big elephant!” she said.
At lunch he finished his payasam, cupped both hands together like a little bowl, and held them up to her.
“More payasam?” she asked. He nodded and bounced. He hardly says words yet, but you could follow him.

qa.q: What passed the gate during the temple festival?
qa.a: The elephant walked past the gate.

qa.q: How can you tell what Gautam was feeling when he stretched his arms wide?
qa.a: His wide arms and look at his mother suggest he was amazed and excited by how big the elephant was, and wanted to share it.

qa.q: How does Gautam's mother help his language grow?
qa.a: She says the meaning aloud each time, "Big elephant!" and "More payasam?", giving him words for his gestures.

qa.q: How does Rajni see Gautam's gestures?
qa.a: Rajni sees that even though he hardly says words yet, his gestures make his meaning easy to follow.

grounding: It shows a toddler stretching his arms wide for big and cupping his hands to ask for more, with an adult naming the meaning aloud.
